At the completion of study a physician has a second birth; he gains the name 'vaidya' not by his former birth; at the completion of learning the brāhma or ārṣa mind surely enters him through knowledge, so the physician is called twice-born.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Āyurveda was revealed by great sages devoted to dharma, desiring the imperishable state, for dharma, artha and kāma. One who practises healing neither for wealth nor for pleasure but out of compassion for beings surpasses all; those who make healing a commodity for livelihood abandon a heap of gold to pursue a heap of dust. There is no gift greater than the gift of life; one who treats thinking compassion for beings the highest dharma attains his aims and the greatest happiness.

paraphrase: The tantra is adorned with thirty-six devices of exposition (tantrayukti) — topic, connection, purpose of reason, meaning of a word, partial statement, enumeration, definition, ellipsis, purpose, instruction, citing a reason, extension, implication, decision, recapitulation, the unqualified and the qualified, exception, the contrary, prima facie view, rule, assent, explanation, doubt, backward and forward reference, technical term, the inferable, aggregation, example, etymology, combination, option, rebuttal, restatement, possibility. As the sun opens a lotus pond and a lamp lights a house, they awaken and illumine a tantra; without them a physician, though studying the texts, does not reach their meaning; a science badly grasped harms the ignorant like a weapon, well grasped it protects.

paraphrase: He in whose heart this saṃhitā of twelve thousand dwells knows meaning and reasoning and is skilled in treatment. What is here is found elsewhere; what is not here is found nowhere.

paraphrase: The eight parts are: surgery (śalya) — removal of foreign bodies and management of wounds with instruments, knives, caustics and fire; śālākya — diseases above the collar-bone (ear, eye, mouth, nose); internal medicine (kāyacikitsā) — diseases of the whole body such as fever, bleeding, consumption, insanity, epilepsy, skin disease, urinary disease and diarrhoea; the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā) — pacifying rites and offerings for those whose minds are seized by gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, ancestors, piśācas, nāgas and grahas; children's medicine; toxicology; rejuvenation (for preserving youth, life, intelligence and strength); and virilization.

paraphrase: The students asked that surgery be made the root of the teaching and that Suśruta put the questions. 'Child Suśruta, the purpose of Āyurveda is the release of the diseased from disease and the protection of the healthy. It is called Āyurveda because in it life is found or by it one attains life. Hear the first and best limb, not contrary to perception, scripture, inference and analogy: it came first, from the healing of wounds and the rejoining of the sacrifice's head — for when Rudra cut off the head of the sacrifice, the gods asked the Aśvins to rejoin it, and they did.'

Brahmā taught it; Prajāpati learnt it from him, the Aśvins from Prajāpati, Indra from the Aśvins, I from Indra; I give it here to those who ask, for the good of creatures. 'I am Dhanvantari, the first god, remover of old age, disease and death for the immortals, come again to earth to teach the limb of surgery with the other limbs.'

paraphrase: In this science the person (puruṣa) is the union of the five great elements with the embodied one (śarīrin); in him treatment takes place, he is its substrate — for the world is twofold, moving and unmoving, and of the four classes of beings (sweat-born, womb-born, egg-born, sprout-born) the person is chief, all else his means.

speaker: Dhanvantari (Divodāsa)

paraphrase: Diseases are what join with suffering; they are fourfold: adventitious (from injury), bodily (rooted in food and drink, from imbalance of vāta, pitta, kapha and blood), mental (anger, grief, fear, elation, dejection, envy, jealousy, misery, malice, lust, greed — distinctions of desire and aversion) and natural (hunger, thirst, old age, death, sleep). They rest in mind and body and are checked by purification, pacification, diet and conduct rightly applied.
speaker: Dhanvantari (Divodāsa)

paraphrase: This is the seed of therapeutics in brief; its exposition will be in one hundred and twenty chapters distributed over five sections — Sūtra, Nidāna, Śārīra, Cikitsita and Kalpa; the remaining matters in the Uttaratantra.
speaker: Dhanvantari (Divodāsa)

paraphrase: The body is rooted in doṣa, dhātu and mala. Vāyu, divided fivefold, marked by moving, carrying, filling, separating and holding, upholds the body; pitta, fivefold, supports it by the action of fire — colour, digestion, ojas, heat, intelligence and warmth; kapha, fivefold, supports it by the action of water — binding the joints, lubrication, healing, filling, strength and firmness.
speaker: Dhanvantari (Divodāsa)

paraphrase: The supreme essence (tejas) of the dhātus from rasa to semen is ojas; that is called strength (bala). Ojas is of the nature of Soma, unctuous, white, cool, stable, flowing, clear, soft and smooth, the best seat of life; the whole body with its parts is pervaded by it, and without it bodies decay. It is diminished by injury, wasting, anger, grief, worry, fatigue and hunger. Its disorders are three — displacement, vitiation and loss — the last ending in fainting, delusion, delirium and death.
speaker: Dhanvantari (Divodāsa)

paraphrase: One whose doṣas, fire, dhātus, wastes and functions are in balance, and whose self, senses and mind are clear, is called healthy (svastha).

paraphrase: Vāta, pitta and śleṣman alone are the causes of the body's origin; unimpaired, set below, in the middle and above, they uphold the body as three pillars uphold a house — hence some call it 'three-pillared'; impaired, they cause its dissolution. With blood as a fourth, they never leave the body in its origin, maintenance and dissolution; the body is never without kapha, pitta, vāyu, nor without blood.
speaker: Dhanvantari (Divodāsa)

paraphrase: As Soma, the Sun and Wind uphold the world by releasing, taking and moving, so kapha, pitta and vāta uphold the body. There is no fire in the body other than pitta: being fiery, pitta is treated like fire in burning and digesting and is called the inner fire. The pitta between the stomachs digests the four kinds of food and separates doṣa, rasa, urine and faeces — the 'digesting fire' (pācaka); that in liver and spleen colours rasa (rañjaka); that in the heart accomplishes what is desired (sādhaka); that in the eye sees (ālocaka); that in the skin gives lustre (bhrājaka).

paraphrase: The doṣas accumulate in their seats (first time for treatment), are provoked (second), spread — singly, in combination or with blood, like a great flood breaking a dike (third), lodge in a particular region (fourth, the prodromal stage), become manifest as a disease (fifth), and become chronic or break open (sixth); untreated they become incurable. 'He who knows accumulation, provocation, spreading, lodging, manifestation and differentiation of the doṣas is a physician'; doṣas removed at accumulation do not go on to the later stages. Blood is never provoked apart from the doṣas.

paraphrase: The cause of all beings, itself uncaused, marked by sattva, rajas and tamas, eightfold in form, the source of the whole world, is the unmanifest (avyakta); it is the one support of many knowers of the field (kṣetrajña), as the ocean of watery things. From it arise the great principle, then ego-sense in three forms; from the sāttvika ego with the taijasa the eleven senses; from the elemental ego the five subtle elements and from them the five great elements — twenty-four principles. The person is the twenty-fifth, conscious when joined with effect and cause; prakṛti and puruṣa share beginninglessness, endlessness, eternity and all-pervasiveness, but prakṛti is one, unconscious and threefold, while the persons are many.
speaker: Dhanvantari (Divodāsa)

paraphrase: Since the effect follows the cause, all these particulars are made of sattva, rajas and tamas, and some say the persons too take on their qualities. But in medicine (vaidyake) the far-sighted hold nature, the Lord, time, chance, destiny and transformation to be the source (prakṛti).

paraphrase: In the Āyurveda treatises the knowers of the field are not taught as all-pervading and eternal; rather, knowers of the field that are not all-pervading are eternal, (born) among animals, men and gods. Their qualities are pleasure and pain, desire and aversion, effort, in- and out-breath, blinking, intellect, mind, resolve, reflection, memory, understanding, determination and perception of objects. Sāttvika qualities are kindness, sharing, forbearance, truth, dharma, faith, knowledge, intellect, memory, steadiness and non-attachment; rājasa and tāmasa their opposites.

paraphrase: Space is rich in sattva, air in rajas, fire in sattva and rajas, water in sattva and tamas, earth in tamas; all interpenetrate, each manifest in its own substance.
speaker: Dhanvantari (Divodāsa)

paraphrase: The constitutions (prakṛti) do not themselves afflict a man, as a worm born in poison is not killed by poison; some call constitution elemental. The mental 'bodies' (kāya) are sixteen: seven sāttvika — of Brahmā (purity, faith, study, honouring the teacher, hospitality, sacrifice), Indra, Varuṇa, Kubera, the Gandharvas, Yama and the ṛṣis; six rājasa — asura, serpent, bird, rākṣasa, piśāca and preta; three tāmasa — beast, fish and plant; knowing them, the physician should treat accordingly.
speaker: Dhanvantari (Divodāsa)

paraphrase: There are one hundred and seven vital points (marma), of five kinds — of flesh, vessels, ligaments, bone and joints; there are no marmas apart from these: eleven of flesh, forty-one of vessels, twenty-seven of ligaments, eight of bone, twenty of joints.
speaker: Dhanvantari (Divodāsa)

paraphrase: All that should be done, rising day after day, by the wise healthy man who wishes to remain free of disease will now be told — beginning with cleaning the teeth with a twig suited to season, doṣa and taste.
speaker: Dhanvantari (Divodāsa)

paraphrase: The wise physician should give rejuvenation in youth or middle age to one whose body has been oleated and purified; a rejuvenative regimen applied to an unpurified body does not shine, like dye applied to a soiled cloth.
speaker: Dhanvantari (Divodāsa)

paraphrase: (The wounded must always be protected from night-wanderers.) One in whom there is knowledge of the hidden and the future, restlessness, intolerance and superhuman action is called seized (sagraha). Grahas strike the impure or those who break bounds, for injury, for sport or for worship; their hosts are countless, but their lords are of eight classes — gods, their enemies, gandharvas, yakṣas, ancestors, serpents, rākṣasas and piśācas.
speaker: Dhanvantari (Divodāsa)

paraphrase: Homage to that unprecedented physician who destroyed all the diseases — passion and the rest — that always cling, spread through the whole body, and cause longing, delusion and discontent.

paraphrase: Brahmā, remembering the Veda of life, taught it to Prajāpati; he to the Aśvins; they to the thousand-eyed (Indra); he to Atri's son and other sages; they to Agniveśa and others, who composed separate tantras; from these, much scattered, this 'Heart of the Eight Limbs' is made, the choicest essence, neither too brief nor too long. Its eight limbs are body (internal medicine), children, seizers (grahas), the parts above the clavicle, surgery, fangs (toxicology), old age (rejuvenation) and virility.
speaker: Vāgbhaṭa

paraphrase: In brief the doṣas are three — vāyu, pitta and kapha; disturbed they destroy the body, undisturbed they sustain it; though pervasive they reside below, between and above the heart and navel, and predominate at the end, middle and beginning of life, day, night and digestion. By them the fire is irregular, sharp or weak, balanced when they are balanced; so too the bowel. As a worm born in poison is not harmed by it, the doṣa predominant in semen and ovum at conception gives the constitution — inferior, middling or best when single, blameable when of two doṣas, best when balanced.
speaker: Vāgbhaṭa

paraphrase: Rasa, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow and semen are the seven dhātus, the 'things to be vitiated'; urine, faeces, sweat and the rest are the malas; all increase by the similar and decrease by the opposite. The tastes are sweet, sour, salt, bitter, pungent and astringent; potency (vīrya) is twofold, hot or cold; post-digestive effect (vipāka) threefold — sweet, sour, pungent; the qualities are twenty: heavy, slow, cold, unctuous, smooth, dense, soft, stable, subtle, clear, with their opposites.
speaker: Vāgbhaṭa

paraphrase: Deficient, wrong and excessive contact of time, objects and action, and their right contact, are the sole causes of disease and health; disease is imbalance of the doṣas, health their balance. Diseases are endogenous or exogenous, their seat body or mind; rajas and tamas are the two doṣas of the mind.

paraphrase: Exercise gives lightness, capacity for work, kindled fire, reduction of fat and well-divided firm limbs; the strong who eat unctuous food should exercise to half their strength in cold seasons and spring, less in others; the vāta- and pitta-afflicted, children, the old and the dyspeptic should avoid it; excess brings thirst, wasting, breathlessness, bleeding, fatigue, cough, fever and vomiting.
speaker: Vāgbhaṭa

paraphrase: All activities of all beings are for the sake of happiness, and there is no happiness without dharma; therefore be devoted to dharma. paraphrase: For the wise the world itself is the teacher in all conduct; in worldly matters follow it with discernment. Tender compassion, giving, restraint of body, speech and mind, and regarding others' interests as one's own — that is the whole of the good vow. One who ever keeps present mindfulness, asking 'how are my nights and days passing, and what have I become?', does not come to suffering.

paraphrase: There are six seasons of two months each from Māgha: late winter, spring, summer, rains, autumn and early winter. The three from late winter make the northern course, the 'taking' period, which daily takes away men's strength: sun and wind, sharp, hot and dry, deplete the earth's cool qualities and the bitter, astringent and pungent tastes grow strong; it is fiery. The rains and the next two make the southern course, the 'releasing' period: the moon is strong, the unctuous sour, salt and sweet tastes prevail; it is cool. Strength is greatest in the cold, least in the rains and summer, middling in the others.
speaker: Ātreya and the other sages

paraphrase: One should not suppress the urges of flatus, faeces, urine, sneezing, thirst, hunger, sleep, cough, breathlessness from exertion, yawning, tears, vomiting and semen.

paraphrase: The body is always upheld by food, sleep and continence rightly used, as a house by its supports. It is diminished by anger, hunger, worry, grief and fatigue; in its loss one is fearful, weak, anxious, with afflicted senses, poor lustre, dejected, dry and emaciated; life-giving herbs, milk and meat-juices are its medicines; with its increase come contentment, nourishment and strength.

paraphrase: Vāyu is fivefold: prāṇa in the head, moving in chest and throat, upholding intellect, heart, senses and mind, governing spitting, sneezing, belching, breathing and swallowing; udāna in the chest, moving in nose, navel and throat, governing speech, effort, energy, strength, complexion and memory; vyāna in the heart, moving through the whole body, governing movement, flexion, extension and blinking; samāna near the fire, which takes, digests, separates and releases food; apāna in the lower region, governing semen, menses, faeces, urine and the delivery of the foetus. Pitta is fivefold: pācaka between the stomachs, which digests food and supports the other pittas; rañjaka in the stomach, colouring rasa; sādhaka in the heart, accomplishing intellect, intelligence and self-regard; ālocaka in the eye; bhrājaka in the skin. Kapha is fivefold: avalambaka in the chest, supporting the other seats of kapha; kledaka in the stomach, moistening food; bodhaka in the tongue, perceiving taste; tarpaka in the head, nourishing the senses; śleṣaka in the joints, binding them.

paraphrase: From rasāyana one gains long life, memory, intelligence, health, youth, excellence of lustre, complexion and voice, strength of body and senses, success of speech, virility and radiance; rasāyana is the means of obtaining the excellent rasa and other dhātus. It should be used in youth or middle age by the self-controlled whose body is oleated, bled and fully purified; rejuvenation or virilization applied to an unpurified body is fruitless, like dye on a dirty cloth.

paraphrase: If diseases arise from a lapse in the rasāyana regimen, treat them with their own remedies, setting rasāyana aside. Know as always on rasāyana one who is truthful, free of anger, with senses turned inward, calm and devoted to good conduct; one endowed with these who takes rasāyana is long-lived and rejoices here and hereafter. Conduct according to the śāstra, attendants who know one's mind, and an intellect unfailing in its aims — that is complete rasāyana.
speaker: Vāgbhaṭa

paraphrase: Asked why some self-possessed patients with every support waste away while others do not, so that the fruit of observing the wholesome seems uncertain, Punarvasu explained: treatment and non-treatment cannot be equal; the physician's art is a hand held out to those sunk in the mire of disease; not all diseases need means, nor are the curable cured otherwise; untimely death is established in all systems — how else could it be warded off by effort? When the four pillars are complete and rightly applied, do not doubt the cure; it is a strong cutter of the noose of death, but nectar in a bad vessel turns to poison; avoid from afar physicians who know only the letter of the texts.
speaker: Vāgbhaṭa

paraphrase: This (science), being established by tradition and seeing its fruit directly, is to be applied like a mantra and is not to be questioned at all.

paraphrase: Brahmā, revealing the Āyurveda that is the essence of the Atharva, made a saṃhitā in his own name of a hundred thousand verses and taught it to Dakṣa Prajāpati; Dakṣa taught the two heavenly physicians, the Aśvins, who made their own saṃhitā; they rejoined Brahmā's head cut off by Bhairava, healed the gods' wounds, Indra's arm, the Moon's consumption, Pūṣan's teeth and Bhaga's eyes, and made Cyavana young; Indra begged Āyurveda from them and taught Ātreya and many sages.

Rasa-knowledge is the supreme knowledge, giving enjoyment and liberation, to be given only to the qualified; success comes to the believer, not to one who says 'it is not'; the slanderer of rasa is reborn for countless births as dog, cat, donkey, crow, worm, cock and vulture, and whoever talks with or touches such slanderers suffers for a thousand births.

The fool who works without serving the guru finds his work fruitless as wealth found in a dream. This great tantra is most rare, to be kept secret, obtained through the guru's grace for the attainment of its fruit; having gained the rasa-works one should not become proud; permitted by the guru, having received the command, one should accomplish the Rasa-Bhairava.

paraphrase: Swooned, mercury removes disease; having experienced binding it gives liberation; well 'killed' it makes immortal — who else is so compassionate as mercury? Herbs dissolve in lead, lead in tin, tin in copper, copper in silver, silver in gold and gold in mercury — as all beings dissolve in the supreme self; this one king of rasas makes the body ageless and deathless. As yogins dissolved in the form of Hara attain immortality, so gold and the metals in the king of rasas that has swallowed mica.

paraphrase: With a stable body, by practice, one gains knowledge with its eight qualities and reaches the state of brahman, free of the suffering of rebirth; the supreme light, three quarters of which are nectar, is not easily gained by dispassion alone. The subtle brahman cannot be worshipped with a body subject to disease, old age and death, perishing in a moment; without a body who could even name the success of yoga? The highest good — beyond sacrifice, giving, austerity, Vedic study, restraint and good conduct — is self-knowledge through yoga.

paraphrase: Even when the bliss of consciousness, free of all conceptions, has flashed forth, what good is it to creatures for one whose body has not shone forth? For some of meritorious vision the conscious light between the eyebrows opens, illuminating the world like fire, lightning or sun: supreme bliss, of the nature of light, free of conception, free of all afflictions, peaceful, self-known; placing the mind there and seeing the whole world as consciousness, one whose bonds of karma are cut attains brahmanhood here itself.
speaker: Govinda

paraphrase: Freed from passion and hatred, truthful in conduct, free of falsehood, people become the same toward all through the touch of consciousness-brahman; those who have attained the deathless state of brahman live on, their bodies shining, joyful, endowed with the subtle powers, their work done. The body is the abode of knowledge and the root of dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa — what higher good is there than an ageless deathless body? A body worn by old age and subject to cough and breathlessness is unfit for samādhi.

paraphrase: Other Māheśvaras, though holding identity with the Supreme Lord, maintain that the jīvanmukti accepted by all will be accomplished only in stability of the body, and so proclaim rasa, called pārada, as the means — pārada because it carries one to the far shore (pāra) of saṃsāra. Liberation in life cannot be had any other way: all six systems place liberation after the fall of the body, where there can be no confidence in it and hence no undoubting effort.

paraphrase: Objection: liberation is accomplished by the manifestation of the supreme reality, being, consciousness and bliss — why this toil to produce a divine body? Reply: that is idle talk, for without a sound body there is no talk of it. The Rasahṛdaya: even when consciousness-bliss has flashed forth, what does it do for creatures to one whose body has not? A body worn by age is unfit for samādhi; a boy of sixteen is greedy for sense-pleasure, and the old man has lost discrimination — how can a mortal attain liberation?

paraphrase: Objection: living (jīvatva) means being in saṃsāra and liberation its opposite — how can they share one seat? Reply: liberation, accepted by all teachers, is either knowable or like a hare's horn; if knowable, life is not to be abandoned, for one who does not live cannot know. Nor is an eternal body unheard of: the followers of Viṣṇusvāmin establish the eternity of Nṛsiṃha's body, being, consciousness and bliss in form.

paraphrase: The body is the abode of all knowledge and the root of dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa; what higher good is there than an ageless, deathless body? Only the lord of rasas can make it so. Its greatness: fruit from seeing and touching it; worship of the mercurial liṅga is more auspicious than all the liṅgas of Kāśī and the rest; and the one who scorns mercury incurs sin and is to be abandoned.

paraphrase: Therefore, having produced the divine body in the way stated, and seen the supreme reality by the power of yoga practice, one attains the goal of man: the conscious light between the brows, illumining the world like fire, lightning and sun, opens for some of meritorious vision — supreme bliss, of the nature of light, free of conception, peaceful, self-known; placing the mind in it and seeing the whole world as consciousness, one whose bonds of karma are cut attains brahmanhood here itself.

paraphrase: A physician skilled in application who has not understood the meaning of the science is to be known as Yama himself, death in the form of mortals. Mercury carries grave natural impurities, each causing its own affliction — swellings, skin disease, burning, loss of seed, death, eruptions and delusion; when mercury is free of impurities it removes death and old age; mercury with its impurities, though nectar itself, is poison. Therefore purification of mercury is enjoined for removing the impurities.

paraphrase: Maheśvara, the first god of the worlds, was born as the great rasa to save the world. The merit of a hundred horse-sacrifices, of crores of cows and thousands of gold gifts, of bathing at all fords, comes from seeing mercury; who worships a mercurial liṅga with devotion gains the fruit of worshipping the liṅgas of the three worlds; eating, touching, giving, meditating on and worshipping mercury — this fivefold worship destroys great sins; whoever scorns the lord of mercury, Śambhu's supreme radiance, falls into a terrible hell; one who gives mercury, purified and properly prepared, to the sick gains the eternal fruit of great gifts and sacrifices.

paraphrase: No science without the right sequence, no sequence without the science; one who acts knowing the science with its sequence succeeds. The teacher of rasa-knowledge is learned, skilled, versed in the rasa-śāstra, accomplished in mantra, heroic, steadfastly devoted to Śiva and the Goddess, knowing all the traditions and skilled in the work. The disciples are devoted to the teacher, of good conduct, truthful, firm in vows, diligent, knowing their own dharma, obedient, free of hypocrisy and envy, initiated, calm and devoted to mantra. Those who are unbelievers, of bad conduct, who cadge from other teachers, or seek the knowledge by theft, deceit or trickery gain no success with gems, mantras or herbs, and if they try out of delusion they destroy their own wealth, finding no happiness here or hereafter; so only when the teacher is pleased by devotion should the disciple receive the rasa-knowledge.

paraphrase: Mercury is not to be used where a vital point (marma) has been severed, nor in burns from caustic or fire. Purified it bears gentle fire; swooned it destroys disease; 'killed' it gives life and health. Poison, fire and dirt are its three natural impurities, causing death, burning and fainting; two from lead and tin cause dullness, distension and skin disease; and seven adventitious 'coverings' (kañcuka), from earth, rock and water, cause skin disease, dullness and wind-disorders — twelve impurities in all, declared by the experts in rasa.
